Schemas dot py now reads the amount as text, a string, with a comment saying why, so the JSON reader's locale-based parsing never touches it. Clean dot py casts that text with try cast to decimal ten two, and a value that was present but did not cast becomes a problem: amount is not a number. Order o ten is now set aside, with a reason, instead of becoming twelve hundred and fifty pounds. Next, a join that quietly doubles revenue.

The stores file has been edited upstream, and somebody added York a second time. Store nine now appears on two lines, both saying York. It looks harmless. Line fourteen joins the completed orders to the stores exactly as Course five did, and line fifteen counts both sides. The terminal says thirteen completed orders, and sixteen rows after the join. Every York order matched both York lines, so every York order now appears twice. Lines sixteen and seventeen sum the sales by city, and York shows a hundred and twenty-five pounds, exactly double its real figure. Nothing failed. Nothing warned. The report would simply be wrong. That is the rule in the table on the right: a join produces one output row for every matching pair. One match per order is what you intend. No match, in an inner join, makes the order vanish, which is what happened to o seven, store fifteen. Two matches double the order. Before trusting a join, you must know the cardinality of the key on the side you are joining to. So the package gets a new module, enrich dot py, with one function, with city, which line nineteen calls. It first groups the stores by store ID and looks for any that appear more than once; if there are, it raises an error naming them, before any order is touched. The end of the terminal shows exactly that: a ValueError, stores dot csv lists store ID nine more than once. Failing is right here: a duplicated reference row is a mistake in somebody else's data, and the people who own that file need to fix it, not have the pipeline guess which York is real. With city also changes the join to a left join, so an order for an unknown store is kept, with a null city, and marked with the problem unknown store, instead of silently disappearing. The stores file is corrected for the next section. Next, two events for the same order.

An event feed records things that happen, and more than one thing can happen to an order. Order o two was completed at four minutes past nine, then refunded at nine-forty. Order o four was sent twice, identically, probably by a retry in the shop's own system. Counting events would count o two as a sale and o four twice. What the report needs is one row per order: its latest state. Grouping by order ID cannot give that, because a group by collapses each group to aggregates and loses the other columns. A window function can. Clean dot py gets a new function, latest, on lines eighteen to twenty-two. Line twenty defines the window: partition by order ID, so each order's events form a group, and order by event time, newest first. Line twenty-one numbers the events within each group with row number, and line twenty-two keeps number one and drops the helper column. The terminal shows the job printing o two's and o four's rows before and after. Every event: o two completed, o two refunded, and o four completed twice at the same time. Latest per order: o two refunded, and o four completed, once. Twenty-one events became nineteen orders. Order o two is no longer a sale, and o four is counted once. The table on the right lists the window functions you will reach for most. Row number numbers rows one, two, three, with no ties. Rank lets ties share a number, so two equal amounts are both first. Lag looks back at the previous row in the window, useful to see what an order's status was before. And any aggregate, such as a sum, can run over a window to give running totals without collapsing the rows. A window is wide, like a group by: every event for an order must meet in one partition, so it costs a shuffle. The two identical o four events are a tie, and row number keeps one of them, which is correct only because they are identical; when events can share a timestamp but differ, add a second sort column. Next, the order at half past eleven at night.

Order o fifteen was placed at twenty-three thirty, UTC, on the first of October. Which day's sales does it belong to? The question sounds trivial and is not, because a timestamp in Spark is an instant, a point on the world's timeline, and an instant has no calendar day until you choose a time zone to look at it from. The table on the right shows o fifteen three ways. In UTC it is the first of October. In London, which in October is on British Summer Time, one hour ahead, it is half past midnight on the second. In New York it is still the first. Until now the job has called to date, which uses the Spark session's time zone, and on this machine that is UTC. So the job has been answering a question nobody asked: which UTC day. The shops close their day in UK time, so the business day is the London day. The new module, summarise dot py, says so in one place. Line five names the shops' time zone. Lines eight to ten define shop day: convert the instant to London wall-clock time with from UTC timestamp, then take its date. And daily sales, from line thirteen, groups completed orders by that shop day and city. The terminal shows both. Order o fifteen's row: event time twenty-three thirty, UTC day the first, shop day the second. And then Leeds, where o fifteen belongs: forty pounds on the first, now one order, and fifty pounds on the second, two orders, because o fifteen has moved to the day it really happened. Two habits follow. Set the session time zone explicitly in configuration rather than inheriting whatever the machine has, because the same job on a laptop in another country would otherwise produce different days. And use timestamp N T Z, the type with no zone, only for wall-clock values that genuinely have none, like a shop's opening hours. Next, data that is not flat: baskets of items.

Not every record is a flat row. The shops also send baskets: for each order, the customer as a nested object, and an array of items, each with a SKU, a quantity and a price. This exploration reads three of them. The schema on lines seven to ten declares the nesting: customer is a struct with an ID and a city, and items is an array of structs. Line thirteen reaches inside: customer dot city picks a field out of the struct, and size counts the items. The terminal shows o one from Leeds with two items, o four from York with one, and o nine from York with none, an empty basket. To work with the items as rows, line fifteen uses explode, which turns each element of the array into a row of its own, repeating the other columns. The terminal reports three rows, from two orders. Order o nine has gone. Explode produces nothing for an empty array, so an order with no items silently disappears. Line eighteen uses explode outer instead, which keeps it with a null item, and gives four rows. That is the first half of the trap. The second is on line twenty. After exploding, the order-level amount is repeated on every item row, so o one's forty pounds now appears twice. Summing it gives ninety-five pounds, for orders worth fifty-five. Exactly the same doubling as the duplicated store, from exactly the same cause: one row became several, and a column that belongs to the order was summed per item. The table on the right lists the three nested types: struct, reached with a dot; array, with size and explode; and map, a set of key-value pairs, reached by key. The rule is to decide the grain of every DataFrame, one row per order or one row per item, and to aggregate only the columns that belong to that grain. Item revenue is quantity times price, summed per item; order revenue is the amount, summed per order. Next, what happens when a transformation needs Python code of its own.

Sometimes no built-in function does what you need, and you write the logic in Python as a user-defined function, a UDF. This exploration converts the European amount, twelve comma fifty, three ways, to show what each costs. The project's requirements now include pandas and pyarrow, for the third way. The first way, on line thirty-one, uses only built-ins: replace the comma with a point using regexp replace, and cast to a decimal. The second, lines fourteen to sixteen, is a Python UDF: an ordinary Python function, decorated with F dot udf and a return type, double. The third, lines nineteen to twenty-one, is a pandas UDF: a function that receives a whole pandas Series at a time and returns one. A helper, operators, collects the names of the operators in each version's physical plan. The terminal shows the results and the plans. All three turned twelve comma fifty into twelve point five. But the built-in gave decimals, forty point zero zero and twelve point five zero, while both UDFs gave floats, because we declared them as double; a UDF's type is whatever you say it is. And the plans differ. The built-in version is just Project and Scan: the whole expression runs inside the JVM, in generated code. The Python UDF adds an operator called Batch Eval Python. That is the boundary: every row is serialised, sent to a Python worker process, run through your function one at a time, and sent back. The pandas UDF adds Arrow Eval Python instead: rows still leave the JVM, but in batches, in Apache Arrow's columnar format, and your function works on whole columns with pandas, which is usually many times faster than the row-at-a-time version. The table on the right sums it up. And there is a cost besides speed: a UDF is a black box, so the optimizer cannot push a filter through it or reason about its result. The rule: built-ins first, a pandas UDF when you must, and a plain Python UDF last. Course ten measures the difference. Next, the checks every run of the job must pass.

Every rule in this course now lives in the package, and the job reads like a description of the pipeline: parse, keep the latest event, add the city, summarise by the shop's day. One question is left. How does a run prove that its output can be trusted? The last module, quality dot py, answers with invariants: statements that must be true of every correct run, checked by the run itself. The check function takes the cleaned orders and the summary. Line eight selects the usable completed orders. Lines nine and ten count them and count their distinct IDs; if the numbers differ, an order is being counted twice, and the run stops. Line twelve checks that no amount is zero or negative. Lines fourteen to seventeen are the strongest check: the money going into the summary must equal the money coming out, to the penny. If a join doubled a row, or a filter lost one, the totals would disagree. Line eighteen counts what was set aside. The terminal shows a real run over all three days. Ten completed orders, each counted once. Every amount positive, and three hundred and sixty-one pounds fifty in equals three hundred and sixty-one pounds fifty out. Five rows set aside with a reason, and the table below lists them: the line that was not valid JSON, o ten whose amount is not a number, o seven for an unknown store, o eight with no amount, and o nine with no status. Those rows are not lost. The job writes them to data slash out slash rejected, as JSON, with their original fields and their problem, so someone can fix them at the source and replay them. The table on the right is the whole course in one view: every flaw in the first day's file, which function handled it, and how. If a future change to the code breaks any of these rules, the run fails before writing a single wrong number, which is exactly what you want from a job nobody watches. Next, Course nine: reading the query plans Spark makes from all this code.

Every query you write passes through four plans before any data moves, and this course reads them. To have something worth planning, the project gets a tool: make orders, in a new tools folder. It uses Spark itself to write a million generated orders, eight Parquet files of them, with fifty stores across five cities, eighty percent of them completed, spread over thirty days. The data is generated with fixed random seeds, so anyone can make exactly the same files, and the terminal shows a million orders in eight files. A second new file, plan view, is a small helper that reads the text explain prints and turns it into data, so the terminal can show plans compactly. This script, plans dot py, runs the pipeline's own summary, daily sales from the summarise module, over the generated orders joined to their stores, and prints each of the four phases as the list of its operators. The table on the right names the phases. The parsed plan is your code turned into a tree, with nothing checked: the quote mark in front of Aggregate means unresolved, a name Spark has not looked up yet. The analyzed plan binds every name to a real column and every function to a real implementation, and checks the types. The optimized plan is the result of rewrite rules that cannot change the answer: here a Project appears just above the parquet read, so only the needed columns are carried, and the filters move down, with an extra check that store ID is not null, since an inner join could never match a null. The physical plan decides how. Its operators are different words: File Scan instead of Relation, Hash Aggregate twice with an Exchange between them, the partial and final sums from Course two, and a Broadcast Hash Join with a Broadcast Exchange, because the stores are small enough to copy to every task. The next sections take these phases one at a time.

The analyzer is the phase that turns text into meaning, and it is also where two classes of bug are caught or quietly introduced. This query, on line nine, is written as SQL: select the order ID and twice the amount from the orders view, where the amount is greater than ninety. But ninety is written in quotes, as a string, the way it often arrives from a configuration file or a web form. Line eleven splits the extended explain output into its sections, and lines twelve and thirteen print the first two. The parsed plan, at the top of the terminal, is exactly what was written. Every name has a quote mark in front of it, because it is only text: tick order ID, tick amount, and the table is an unresolved relation called orders. Nothing has been checked; a typo would look identical. The analyzed plan, below it, has resolved everything, and the table on the right lists what changed. The output schema appears first: order ID a string, doubled a decimal twelve two. Order ID has become order ID hash zero, a specific column with an ID that the rest of planning uses. The unresolved relation has become the view, and beneath it the Parquet relation it stands for. The multiplication has an explicit cast, two as a decimal. And then the line to look at twice. The comparison amount greater than the string ninety has become cast amount as double, greater than cast ninety as double. To compare a decimal with a string, Spark's type rules converted both sides to floating point. For ninety it makes no difference, but for a boundary like nineteen point nine nine, a double comparison can land on the wrong side, and the decimal's exactness, which we fought for in Course eight, is gone without a word. The fix is to compare like with like: amount greater than ninety, as a number, keeps the decimal. Reading the analyzed plan is how you catch such conversions before they cost money. Next, the optimizer, and the join it chooses.

Two kinds of decision happen after analysis. The optimizer rewrites the logical plan by rules that never change the result, and the planner then chooses physical strategies, where the choice changes the cost enormously. This script shows one of each. Lines sixteen to eighteen pull two facts out of the plan's File Scan. Pushed filters lists the conditions handed down to the Parquet reader: status is not null and equals completed, and store ID is not null. The reader uses them to skip whole row groups whose statistics show they cannot match. And the read schema lists the columns actually read: store ID, amount, status and event time. The order ID is never read at all, because nothing downstream uses it. That is column pruning, and on a columnar format it means those bytes never leave the disk. Then the strategy. Lines nineteen to twenty-three plan the same summary twice, with the setting auto broadcast join threshold first at its default of ten megabytes, then at minus one, which switches broadcasting off. Notice the function on line twelve: a DataFrame keeps the physical plan it made the first time, so changing a setting afterwards does nothing to it, and the script builds a fresh DataFrame each time. With the default, the plan has a Broadcast Hash Join, a Broadcast Exchange, and one Exchange for the aggregation: the stores file is tiny, so Spark copies it whole to every task, and the million orders never move for the join. With broadcasting off, Spark falls back to a Sort Merge Join, and there are now three Exchanges: both sides shuffled by store ID so matching rows meet, then the aggregation's. The table on the right lists the strategies and what each moves. Spark picks broadcast when it estimates one side is under the threshold; Course ten looks at what happens when its estimate is wrong. Next, how the physical plan is turned into running code.

A physical plan is still a description. To run it, Spark compiles it, and the asterisk numbers in the plan show how. This script turns Adaptive Query Execution off on line ten, so the plan is shown exactly as compiled before running, and prints two things. First, line fourteen asks for the code generation explain mode, whose first line reports that Spark found three whole-stage code generation subtrees. Second, line fifteen prints the physical plan's shape. Every operator marked with asterisk two in brackets, the File Scan's columnar-to-row conversion, the filter, the project, the broadcast hash join, the project and the partial hash aggregate, has been fused into one generated Java function. Instead of each operator handing rows to the next through a virtual function call, Spark writes a single tight loop that reads a row, filters it, looks up its store, and adds it to the running sum, and compiles that loop at runtime. That is whole-stage code generation, and it is a large part of why DataFrame code is fast. Asterisk one is the small filter on the stores, and asterisk three is the final aggregation. An Exchange always ends a fused subtree, because data has to be written out and read back in. The last line reads the executor's memory from Spark's monitoring API: four hundred and thirty-four mebibytes of unified memory, out of the one gibibyte heap the driver gets by default. The table on the right shows where that number comes from. Spark reserves three hundred mebibytes for itself; of the rest, sixty percent, spark dot memory dot fraction, is unified memory, shared by execution, for shuffles, joins, sorts and aggregations, and storage, for cached data. Execution can take memory from storage when it needs to, evicting cached blocks, and when even that is not enough, it spills to disk, which Course ten measures. The other forty percent is left for your own objects. Next, the cuts in the plan, and the stages they become.

The physical plan now gets matched to what actually ran. This script, again with adaptive execution off so the plan is the one written, prints the plan's shape, runs the summary with collect on line fourteen, and then asks the monitoring API for every stage the application ran, with its tasks and the bytes it wrote to and read from the shuffle. The top of the terminal is the plan, and its one hash Exchange is the cut. Below the cut, asterisk two: scan, filter, broadcast join and partial aggregate. Above it, asterisk three: the final aggregate. The broadcast exchange, folded here, feeds the join from the side. Then the stages that ran. Stage zero, one task, and stage one, one task: small jobs Spark ran for itself, the first reading the Parquet files' footers to learn their schema, the second collecting the stores so they could be broadcast. Stage two is the cut's lower half, drawn on the right: four tasks, one per input split of the eight files, each scanning its share, joining every order to its city through the broadcast copy, computing partial sums per day and city, and writing them to the shuffle: seventeen thousand four hundred and sixty-four bytes in all. Stage three is the upper half: two hundred tasks, one per shuffle partition, reading exactly those seventeen thousand bytes back and finishing the sums. A million orders went in; seventeen kilobytes crossed the shuffle, because the partial aggregation shrank them to one row per day, city and task before anything moved. That is the shape of a healthy plan. And there is the familiar waste: two hundred tasks to finish a result that is a hundred and fifty rows. Next, the same query with adaptive execution switched back on, and the plan it ends up with.

Spark has been on its best behaviour so far, because twice now we switched Adaptive Query Execution off to see the plan as written. This script leaves it on, its default, runs the summary, and then does something important: it reads the plan after the action. With adaptive execution, the plan explain shows before running is a starting point, and the one after running is what actually happened. The terminal shows a hundred and fifty rows, thirty days times five cities, and the top of the final plan. It is now marked as a result query stage, and under the final hash aggregate there is a new operator, AQE shuffle read, reading from a shuffle query stage. Adaptive execution split the query into stages it runs one at a time, and between them it looks at the real statistics of what the previous stage produced, then re-plans the rest. The trace below is the monitoring API's account. Stages zero and one are the footer read and the broadcast, as before. Stage two is the map side, four tasks, writing the same seventeen thousand four hundred and sixty-four bytes. Stage three is marked skipped: it was planned, then made unnecessary. And stage four ran the final sums with one task, reading all seventeen thousand bytes. Having seen that the whole shuffle was seventeen kilobytes, adaptive execution coalesced the two hundred shuffle partitions into one, instead of starting two hundred tasks to read a few hundred bytes each. The table on the right sets it beside the last section. It can also switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast join once it sees a side is small, and split a skewed partition, which Course ten shows. Two habits follow. Read plans after the action, not only before. And when a plan surprises you, read the trace: the stages, their task counts and their shuffle bytes say what ran, not what was intended. Next, Course ten: making the job fast, with measurements to prove it.

Before making anything faster, you need a number to beat, and a way to know the faster version still gives the same answer. This course measures everything on ten million generated orders, ten times Course nine's million, on this machine: four cores, fifteen gigabytes of memory, Spark in local mode with four task slots. The terminal first generates them, eight Parquet files, then runs the baseline script. The new file in the editor, tools slash bench dot py, is the measuring kit, and every number in this course comes through it. Seconds, from line nine, runs an action once and throws that time away, because the first run pays for things later runs do not: JVM code warming up, files coming into the operating system's cache, Python workers starting. Then it runs the action three more times and returns the median, which a single slow run cannot drag around. Run, folded here, executes a DataFrame completely with a write to the noop format, a sink that discards everything, so we time the computation and not printing or disk writes. And checksum, from line twenty-five, reduces a result to its row count and its total sales. The terminal shows the baseline: ten million orders in eight files; a checksum of a hundred and fifty rows and four hundred and twenty million pounds; and a median of about two and a half seconds for the whole daily summary. Remember that the timing is not exact. Run the script again and it will say two point three, or two point nine. On a shared machine, differences of a few tenths of a second are noise, and part of measuring is knowing the size of your noise before believing any improvement smaller than it. The table on the right lists the rules this course keeps: representative data, a discarded warm-up, the median of three, a checksum on every variant, and the machine stated with every number. Next, finding where the two and a half seconds go.

The web interface on port four thousand and forty is the usual way to see where a job spends its time, and everything it shows comes from the monitoring API this script reads directly. Line twelve runs the daily summary once. Lines fifteen to twenty then fetch every stage of the application and print them sorted by run time, slowest first, with the number of tasks, the run time, the megabytes read from input files, and the kilobytes written to the shuffle. The terminal makes the answer obvious. Stage two takes almost all of the time: four tasks, about sixteen and a half thousand milliseconds of run time, reading forty-five megabytes, and writing seventeen kilobytes to the shuffle. Every other stage is a fraction of a second or nothing: the footer read, the broadcast of the stores, the final aggregation, and a stage that was planned and skipped. Two details help read these numbers correctly. Run time is summed over all of a stage's tasks, so sixteen seconds of task time spread over four cores in parallel is about four seconds of wall time, and some of that overlaps other work; it is not the elapsed time of the stage. And the input of forty-five megabytes is less than the ninety megabytes of files, because Parquet read only the four columns the query needs. The table on the right says what each metric tells you. The lesson is the order of work. Find the expensive stage before changing anything. Here it is the scan, filter, broadcast join and partial aggregation, fused into stage two, so that is where any improvement must come from. Tuning the shuffle, with only seventeen kilobytes crossing it, would be work spent on the one part of the job that costs nothing. Next, symptoms that show a stage is struggling, starting with spill.

When a stage is slow, the metrics usually say why, and each kind of trouble has its own signature. This script produces the clearest one on purpose. Lines fourteen to seventeen sort all ten million orders by amount, twice: first with the shuffle forced into a single partition, then into two hundred. With adaptive execution off, so the settings are honoured as written. After each run, line nineteen reads the last stage's disk bytes spilled. With one partition, a single task had to sort every row, and the terminal shows that it spilled a hundred and fifty megabytes to disk: its share of memory ran out, so it sorted in pieces, wrote them to disk, and merged them back. That task ran for over twenty seconds. With two hundred partitions, each task sorted a two-hundredth of the rows, everything fitted in memory, nothing spilled, and the total task time dropped by several seconds even though there was much more task overhead. Spill is the memory symptom. The table on the right lists the others and where to look for each. A CPU-bound stage shows run time close to the task time, and if garbage collection time is a large share of it, objects are churning. An I/O-bound stage shows large input or shuffle read bytes relative to its run time. A scheduling problem shows a stage with fewer tasks than slots, so cores sit idle, or thousands of tiny tasks whose run time is mostly start-up. And one slow task among many fast ones, which the task-time quantiles reveal, is skew, the subject of section seven. The remedy for spill is rarely more memory. It is giving each task less data, with more partitions, or making the data smaller before the wide operation. Next, choosing the number of partitions.

Spark's default of two hundred shuffle partitions is a guess made without seeing your data, and this script measures what other guesses cost. It needs an aggregation where the shuffle carries real volume, so line nine groups the ten million orders by order ID, which produces ten million groups, every row its own. Adaptive execution is off on line seven, so each setting is used exactly as given. The loop on lines eleven to fourteen sets the number of shuffle partitions and times the aggregation, a median of three runs after a warm-up, for four, sixteen, two hundred and two thousand partitions. The terminal shows a curve with a floor. Four partitions took about eight seconds: each task handled two and a half million groups, and with only four tasks for four cores there was no slack, so the slowest task set the pace. Sixteen was fastest, at about six and a half seconds. Two hundred, the default, was close behind at seven and a half. And two thousand was slowest of all, at about twelve seconds: each task did almost nothing, so the cost of scheduling, starting and finishing two thousand tasks, and of writing and reading two thousand pieces of shuffle, outweighed the work. The table on the right sets out why. The best number is not a constant; it depends on the volume crossing the shuffle and the number of cores. A useful rule of thumb is to size partitions, not to count them: aim for shuffle partitions of roughly a hundred to two hundred megabytes, enough of them to keep every core busy in a few waves, and no more. On our production cluster of two hundred slots, that is a very different number from sixteen. And this is exactly the decision adaptive execution makes at runtime, by coalescing small partitions after it has seen the real sizes, which is why it is on by default. Next, changing the partitioning yourself: repartition and coalesce.

Sometimes you need to change how many partitions a DataFrame has, usually to control how many files a write produces, and Spark gives two tools with very different costs. This script writes the completed orders four ways and reports, for each, the number of files written, the time, and whether the plan contains an Exchange, meaning a shuffle. As read, the eight input files arrived as four partitions, so the write produced four files in about four and a half seconds, with no shuffle. Repartition sixteen shuffled every row to produce sixteen evenly sized partitions: sixteen files, in about eleven seconds, more than double, because every row was written to the shuffle and read back before it could be written to Parquet. Coalesce two merged the existing partitions into two without moving rows between machines: two files, no shuffle, about six seconds, slower than as read only because two tasks now did the work of four. And coalesce one: one file, no shuffle, about eleven seconds, as slow as the repartition, because a single task did everything, the reading, the filtering and the writing, on one core while three sat idle. The listing at the bottom shows the single part file. The table on the right sets the two tools side by side. Repartition always shuffles, can raise or lower the count, and gives even partitions. Coalesce never shuffles, can only lower the count, and keeps whatever imbalance the input had; and because it avoids a stage boundary, it reduces the parallelism of everything upstream in the same stage, not only the write. Hence the one-file trade in the list. A single output file is sometimes required, for a tool that cannot read a folder. Coalesce one buys it by putting the whole job on one core. On a large result, write in parallel and merge files afterwards if you truly must. Next, the join strategies, measured.

Course nine showed the planner choosing a broadcast hash join for our stores. This script measures what that choice is worth, by forcing each strategy in turn with a join hint. First, lines ten to twelve ask for the cost explain mode, which includes the planner's size estimates. Spark estimated the orders at about ninety-one mebibytes, the size of the Parquet files, and the stores at five hundred and five bytes. That second number is why the default plan broadcasts: anything estimated under the ten megabyte threshold is copied whole to every task. Then the loop on lines fourteen to eighteen joins the orders to the stores with three hints. Broadcast gives a broadcast hash join in under two seconds. Shuffle hash gives a shuffled hash join: both sides are shuffled by store ID and the smaller side's partition is built into a hash table in each task, about four seconds. Merge gives a sort-merge join, in which both sides are shuffled and then sorted, so that matching keys can be walked through in step, about five seconds. The table on the right sums up what each one moves. The broadcast moves five hundred bytes, once, and the ten million orders stay where they are. The two shuffle joins move all ten million orders across the shuffle, and sort-merge also sorts them. Sort-merge is still the right strategy when both sides are large, because it never needs either side to fit in memory; that robustness is why it is Spark's default for large joins. The lesson is to know which join you are getting, from the plan, and why, from the estimates. Hints exist to correct the planner when you know better, for instance when an estimate is badly wrong, but a hint is also a promise that can go stale as data grows, and a broadcast of something that has quietly grown to gigabytes can take a driver down. Next, the data that defeats every strategy: skew.

Real data is rarely even. In this version of the generated orders, written by make orders with the skewed option, store seven is a flagship that takes half of all ten million orders. The script joins the orders to a small per-store table with a shuffle, broadcasting switched off on line thirteen and partition coalescing off on line fourteen, so we see the two hundred partitions as they are. A shuffle sends every row with the same key to the same partition, so store seven's five million rows all land in one task. For each attempt, the script reads the join stage's task-time quantiles from the monitoring API: the median task, the slowest task, and the largest partition. The plain join shows the problem plainly: a median task of about ten milliseconds, a slowest task of nearly five seconds, and a largest partition of sixty-eight megabytes. One task did half the work while a hundred and ninety-nine waited. The second attempt turns on adaptive execution's skew join, which can split an oversized partition into several tasks. It changed nothing, and the reason is in the numbers: it only treats a partition as skewed above two hundred and fifty-six megabytes, and five times the median, by default. Sixty-eight megabytes is under its threshold. The third attempt salts the join, on lines eighteen to twenty-one. Each order gets a random salt from zero to fifteen, and the small table is repeated sixteen times, once per salt, so the join key becomes store and salt. Store seven's rows are now spread over sixteen keys, and so over up to sixteen tasks: the slowest task dropped to about half a second, ten times faster, with the largest partition at seven megabytes. The table on the right lists the other remedies. And the lesson is in the list: the slowest task sets the pace of a stage, and averages hide it, so read quantiles. Next, caching: when keeping data is cheaper than recomputing it.

Every action reruns its whole plan, as Course two showed. Caching keeps a DataFrame's rows after the first time they are computed, so the next action can start from them. It sounds like free speed, and this script measures whether it is. Line eleven keeps the completed orders' store and amount, and line twelve sums them per store. Line fourteen times that summary the usual way, recomputed from the Parquet files every run. Line fifteen caches the completed orders and runs a count, because a cache is only filled by an action. Line sixteen times the same summary again, now reading the cached rows. The terminal shows the result honestly: about one second recomputed, and about point nine of a second cached. The cache saved a tenth of a second, within the noise of this machine. And the last line, from the storage part of the monitoring API, shows what it cost: four cached partitions, sixty-nine megabytes of memory, taken from the same unified pool that execution uses for shuffles and sorts. Why so little gain? Because what we cached was cheap to recompute. Reading two columns of a Parquet file is fast, columnar and compressed, and the filter on top of it is trivial. Caching it mostly replaced one fast read with another, slightly faster one. The list on the right is the rule that follows. Cache a DataFrame that is reused by several actions and expensive to produce: the result of a big join, a heavy clean-up with window functions, or a shuffle you would otherwise repeat. Do not cache straight after a read. Unpersist when you are done, because cached data competes with execution for memory, and a job that caches too much spills more. The table lists the storage levels: DataFrames default to memory and disk, spilling what does not fit. Next, the cheapest data to process: the data you never read.

The fastest bytes are the ones never read, and how data is laid out on disk decides how many you can skip. This script writes the ten million orders two new ways and asks each layout for something. Line thirteen adds a day column, and line fourteen writes the orders partitioned by day, a folder for each of the thirty days. Line fifteen writes the same orders as two thousand small files. Then, for each layout, the loop asks the monitoring API how many bytes the stages read and how many tasks they ran. The terminal shows the answers. Reading one day from the original layout, a single folder, read ninety-one point six megabytes in four tasks: every file had to be opened, because the day is inside the files. Parquet's statistics could skip some blocks, but the event times are spread through every file. Reading the same day from the by-day layout read three point three megabytes in a single task: partition pruning, from Course six, at scale. Spark saw from the folder names alone that only one folder held the seventh of October, and never touched the other twenty-nine. Twenty-eight times less data, without a line of query code changing. And the two thousand small files, filtered for amounts over ninety-nine, read three hundred and forty-eight megabytes in sixty-three tasks: almost four times the bytes of the original. The reason: repartitioning into two thousand pieces shuffled the rows randomly, and random rows compress much worse than rows written in order; and every file adds its own footer and its own listing cost. The list on the right sums up the rules. Partition output by what readers filter on. Keep files reasonably large, hundreds of megabytes, not a few kilobytes each. And remember that the order rows are written in affects compression, so a sort before a write can shrink both storage and every later scan. Next, adaptive execution, changing a plan while it runs.

A planner can only be as good as its estimates, and some estimates cannot be made in advance. Line eight keeps the orders with an amount over ninety-nine point nine. How many is that? Spark does not know: without statistics on the column, it assumes a filter keeps a large share of the rows, so it estimates this side of the join as roughly the size of the whole table. Line nine joins it to all ten million orders by order ID and counts per store. The terminal's first line is the plan before running: a sort-merge join, the safe choice for two big sides. Line eighteen runs the query, and line nineteen reads the plan again. Now the first join listed is a broadcast hash join; the sort-merge join still appears, second, because explain prints the final plan and then the initial one. The last line shows why: nine thousand nine hundred and five rows came through that filter, about a tenth of one percent. Adaptive execution ran the filter side as its own query stage, saw that its real size was far under the ten megabyte broadcast threshold, and replanned the join as a broadcast before the expensive part of the work began. Nobody had to add a hint, and a hint would have been wrong on another day's data anyway. The table on the right lists what adaptive execution does with the facts it gathers between stages: it coalesces tiny shuffle partitions, as in Course nine; it switches joins to broadcast, as here; it splits skewed partitions, above the thresholds we met in section seven; and it removes work whose input turns out to be empty. It is on by default in Spark four, and the main reason to turn it off is the one we used: to study a plan exactly as written. When you read a plan to diagnose a problem, read it after the action. Next, the resources a job runs on.

Everything so far ran on four task slots. This script asks what the slots are worth, by running the same daily summary on one, two and four of them. Each turn of the loop on lines eleven to sixteen starts a fresh local session with that many cores, times the summary, and stops. The terminal shows about five seconds on one core, about three on two, and under two on four. Doubling the cores from one to two nearly halved the time; doubling again saved less. Four cores were roughly two and a half to three times as fast as one, not four times, because some of the work is not parallel at all: starting the job, planning it, broadcasting the stores, the final single-task aggregation, and the moments when one task is still running while the others have finished. That shape, fast early gains and diminishing returns, holds on a cluster too, and it is why adding executors is not a substitute for a better plan. On a cluster you size executors with the settings in the table on the right. Executor cores are the task slots in each executor; executor memory is its heap; the number of instances fixes how many executors a static allocation starts; and memory overhead is the off-heap allowance per executor, by default the larger of three hundred and eighty-four megabytes and ten percent of the heap, which container managers count against the limit. A common shape is four or five cores per executor, which keeps each executor's tasks sharing memory sensibly. Dynamic allocation, in the list, lets the number of executors follow the work: Spark requests more while tasks are queued and releases executors that sit idle. For that to be safe, shuffle files must survive their executor, so it needs either an external shuffle service or shuffle tracking. Next, putting the course together: one change at a time, with the checksum every time.

The last section of this course is about the claims you make with numbers, because a performance change is only real if the evidence for it is. This script compares four configurations of the daily summary. Each starts from Spark's defaults, on lines seventeen and eighteen, applies exactly one change, rebuilds the query, and records the median time and the checksum. The terminal shows them. The baseline, with the defaults: about two point nine seconds. Adaptive execution off: about two point five. Sixteen shuffle partitions: about two point three. And two thousand partitions with adaptive execution off: about six and a half seconds. All four checksums are identical: a hundred and fifty rows and the same four hundred and twenty million pounds to the penny, so every variant computes the same answer. Now read the times with the noise in mind. In the first section the same baseline took two and a half seconds; here it took two point nine. Differences of half a second between these first three rows are inside that noise, so this run does not support the claim that sixteen partitions or turning adaptive execution off makes the job faster. What the numbers do support is the last row: two thousand partitions without adaptive execution's coalescing is about three times slower, far outside the noise, for the reason section four measured. The table on the right sets out which claims hold. And the list is the discipline for any performance work. Change one thing at a time, from the same baseline. Prove the result is identical. Know the size of your noise before believing a small gain. And state the machine, the data and the version, because none of these numbers will hold unchanged on a fifty-executor cluster, and the honest summary of an experiment on one machine says so. That finishes the batch job. Next, Course eleven: the same summary, computed continuously as events arrive.

So far every job has read a day of orders that was complete before the job began. That data is bounded: it has an end, and the job reads all of it. A live feed of orders never ends. It is unbounded, and this course turns the daily summary into a query that keeps up with it. Two new pieces make that possible. tools slash feed dot py plays the day back: the shops' events arrive as four files, ten events in all, and deliver copies the next one into an inbox folder, data slash stream slash in. And pipeline slash session dot py gains build stream session, which sets four shuffle partitions, because a streaming query fixes its state's partitioning on its first run. Now the query. Line thirteen is the only change you have to make to the source: spark dot read stream instead of spark dot read. It is the same schema and the same clean dot parse, but it describes a folder to watch, not a file to read. Line fifteen is the same group by and sum as the batch job. What is different is how it runs. Lines twenty-six and twenty-seven start the query each time a file arrives, and the terminal shows the result after each one. After the first file, store seven has sixty-five pounds and store nine fifteen. After the second, the totals grow, and store twelve appears. Spark did not re-read the first file to get there: it read only the new rows and added them to the totals it kept from the last batch. That memory is called state, and the rest of the course is largely about it. Look closely at store seven after the second file: ninety, not sixty-five. The second file contains order o two again, resent by the shop, and this query counts it twice. A batch job could deduplicate the whole day; a stream has to remember what it has seen, and section eight measures what that memory costs. Next, what the engine records about each of these batches.

A streaming query in Spark is not a different engine. It is the same planner and the same executors, run again and again on small slices of new data called micro-batches. This script asks the engine for its own account of each one. Line seventeen writes to the noop sink, which computes everything and keeps nothing, because only the record of each batch matters here. After each run, line twenty-one reads the query's last progress, a dictionary that Spark fills in for every micro-batch it completes. Lines twenty-two and twenty-three pull out two fields from it: the source's end offset, and the number of rows held as state. The terminal shows the four batches. The first file brings three rows in, the source offset is zero, and the aggregation holds two rows of state: one running total for store seven and one for store nine. The second file brings three rows and moves the offset to one, and the state grows to three rows as store twelve appears. The last two files bring two rows each, and the state stays at three, because no new store appears. That is the important thing about the state here: it grows with the number of stores, not with the number of orders. The table on the right lists the fields that were read, and one we will need soon, the watermark. The list sets out what one micro-batch does, in order. The engine asks the source what is new, as an offset range. It writes that range into the checkpoint before it runs anything, so that a crash can be replayed exactly. It runs the plan on just those rows, updating the state. And it hands the result to the sink and commits the batch. That order, plan the range, record it, run, commit, is what every guarantee later in this course depends on. Next, what the source and the sink at either end promise.

Before going further, it helps to know what each end of a streaming query promises, because the guarantees of the whole pipeline are only as strong as the weaker end. On the left are the two ends this course uses. The source is a folder: spark dot read stream, with the order schema, reading JSON from data slash stream slash in. The sink, in the job we finish with, is a folder of Parquet files written in append mode with a checkpoint location. On the right are the tables from the Structured Streaming guide for Spark four point zero point one; nothing on this frame was measured, it is what the guide promises. A source is safe if it can replay: read exactly the same data again from a position it records. The file source can, because it remembers which files it has already read. Kafka can, because a topic keeps offsets. The rate source, which generates rows for testing, can too. The socket source cannot: once a line has been read from the socket, it is gone, so it is for experiments only. A sink is judged by what happens when a batch is written twice, which is exactly what a restart after a crash does. The file sink is exactly once: it records which batches it has committed, so a replayed batch is not written again. Kafka is at least once: a replay can publish the same records twice. foreach batch is whatever your code makes it, and section twelve shows both outcomes. Console and memory keep nothing, so they are for debugging. The list states the rule. End-to-end exactly once needs three things together: a source that can replay, a checkpoint that records which offsets each batch took, and a sink that is idempotent, so writing a batch twice changes nothing. Lose any one of the three, and a crash means lost rows or doubled rows. The rest of this course uses the file source, and every guarantee it shows rests on that replay.

A trigger decides when a streaming query runs its next micro-batch. It never changes what the query computes; only how the work is sliced. This script makes that visible. Before it starts any query, it delivers all four files, so all ten events are already waiting. Then it reads the folder twice. The first read, on line thirteen, has no limit. The second, on line fifteen, sets max files per trigger to one, so each micro-batch may take at most one file. Both queries are run once with the available now trigger, through tools slash feed dot py, and line twenty-five counts the batches in the query's recent progress. The terminal shows the result. With no limit, available now runs a single batch of ten rows. With one file per trigger, it runs four batches, of two, two, three and three rows, and then stops. The sizes are sorted on line twenty-five, because four files that land together may be taken in any order. The table on the right lists the triggers in Spark four point zero point one. With no trigger at all, the next batch starts as soon as the last one ends. A processing time trigger, such as one minute, starts a batch on that interval, when there is new data. Available now processes everything waiting when the query starts, in as many batches as the limits allow, and then stops, which is how this course runs every query and how a scheduled streaming job runs cheaply. The older once trigger is deprecated in its favour. And the continuous trigger, which processes rows one at a time with a checkpoint interval, is still experimental, supports only map-like queries, and gives only at-least-once guarantees, so this course does not use it. The list sums up. A trigger decides when, a limit decides how much, and the same input gives the same answer either way. Next, the most important question about a stream: which time do we mean?

Every order has two times. Event time is when it happened, recorded by the shop in the event itself. Processing time is when Spark saw it, which depends on networks, on retries and on when the job ran. In a batch job over a finished day the difference hardly matters. In a stream it is the whole problem. This script shows the gap directly. There is no aggregation: each micro-batch hands its new rows to the show function on line sixteen, which sorts them by event time and prints each order with the time it happened. The terminal shows the four batches. The first holds o one, o two and o three, from nine oh one to nine oh eight. The second holds o four and o five, and o two again, resent. Then the third batch brings o six, at nine twenty-three, and o seven, at nine oh six: an order that happened seventeen minutes before the one that arrived ahead of it. And the last batch brings o eight, at nine thirty-one, and o nine, at nine oh two, nearly half an hour late. The table on the right lines them up. Every late order is a real event that a shop sent late, perhaps because its network was down. The list states the consequence. When the business asks for sales at nine o'clock, it means orders that happened at nine o'clock, not orders that happened to arrive then. So the query has to group by event time, and it has to decide what to do with an order that arrives after its time has been reported. Grouping by processing time would be simpler, and wrong: o seven would be counted in the wrong ten minutes. Next, windows of event time, and what a late order does to them.

A window is a group of event time. Line fourteen groups the orders by window of event time, ten minutes, so each order falls into exactly one window: nine o'clock up to ten past, ten past up to twenty past, and so on. Line fifteen sums the amounts in each. The query runs in complete mode, so every batch emits every window it knows about, and the terminal shows them. Follow the nine o'clock window across the four batches, which the table on the right sets out. After the first file it holds eighty pounds: o one, o two and o three. After the second it holds a hundred and five, because o two was resent and counted again. After the third it holds a hundred and thirty-five: o seven, at nine oh six, arrived late but still landed in the window it belongs to. And after the fourth it holds a hundred and forty, when o nine, half an hour late, is added too. This is event time doing its job: a late order updates the window it belongs to, not the one that is current when it arrives. But look at what that costs. Because any order might still arrive late, Spark can never say that the nine o'clock window is finished. It keeps every window open, in state, for ever, and a query that runs for months keeps months of windows. Complete mode makes it worse, re-emitting every window on every batch. The list sums it up. Windows by event time are correct, but with no limit on lateness they are never final and their state never shrinks. The engine needs to be told how late is too late, and that is the watermark.

A watermark is the query's answer to how late is too late. Line fourteen adds one: with watermark on event time, ten minutes. From then on, the watermark is the latest event time the query has seen, minus ten minutes, and anything older than it may be treated as finished. The query writes in append mode, on line twenty-seven, which emits each window exactly once, when it is final, and never changes it afterwards. The terminal shows the watermark after every batch. Notice that each file produces two batches: one that processes the data, and one with no data that only moves the watermark forward, because the new watermark is computed from the batch that just ran. The table on the right gives the arithmetic. After the first file the latest event is nine oh eight, so the watermark is eight fifty-eight. After the second it is nine oh seven, after the third nine thirteen, and after the fourth nine twenty-one. The nine o'clock window ends at ten past nine, so it becomes final in batch five, when the watermark passes nine thirteen. It is emitted then, once, with a hundred and thirty-five pounds. The ten past window is emitted in batch seven, at a hundred and forty. Now compare that to the last section. There, the nine o'clock window reached a hundred and forty. Here it is a hundred and thirty-five, and the difference is o nine. o seven, at nine oh six, arrived when the watermark was nine oh seven, but its window was still open, so it counted. o nine, at nine oh two, arrived after the window had been emitted as final, so Spark dropped it. That is the trade a watermark makes, stated in the list: a window becomes final, state can be released, and an order later than the bound is let go. Ten minutes is a business decision, not a technical one. Next, what that bound does to the state.

Section one counted o two twice. The fix is to drop duplicates, and in a stream that means remembering every order id the query has seen. This script measures what that memory costs, two ways. Line thirteen is drop duplicates on order id, with no watermark: the stream equivalent of the batch job's fix. Lines fourteen and fifteen add a ten-minute watermark and use drop duplicates within watermark, which keeps an order id only for as long as a duplicate of it could still arrive. Both run to the noop sink, and line twenty-two reads the number of rows each holds as state. The terminal and the table show the result. After the first two files, both hold the same: three ids, then five, because the watermark has not yet moved far enough to release anything. After the third file they part. Without a watermark the state is seven rows, one for every distinct order so far. With one it is five: the earliest orders are now older than the watermark, so their ids are dropped from memory. After the last file, nine rows against four. On ten orders that is nothing. But the two curves have different shapes. Without a watermark, state grows with every order ever seen, and the retail chain sends two hundred gigabytes of events a day. With one, state holds only the last stretch of time, however long the query runs. The list says where that state lives: on the executors, in memory, and copied into the checkpoint on every batch, so that a restart can reload it. A stream with unbounded state is a job that slowly runs out of memory and gets slower to checkpoint every day. So every stateful operation in a long-running query needs a bound, and the watermark is how you give it one. Next, the output modes, and which queries each allows.

An output mode decides which rows of the result a micro-batch hands to the sink. This script runs the same windowed query, with its ten-minute watermark, three times, once in each mode. The counter function on line twenty-one adds up how many rows each mode writes, and lines twenty-nine to thirty-one run all three after each file. The terminal shows the running totals. Append writes nothing for the first two files, because no window is final yet, then one row after the third file and one more after the fourth: two rows in all, each a finished window, written exactly once. Update writes every window that changed in a batch: one, then three, then five, then six. And complete writes the whole result table every time: one, three, six and ten, growing with every batch. The second table on the right says when to use each one. Append is the mode for files, and for any sink that can only add: each row is written once and never revised. That is why it needs a watermark when there is an aggregation, because without one no window would ever be final and append would write nothing at all. Update writes the rows that changed, so the sink has to be able to replace a row by its key: a database table, or a merge into a table format. Complete rewrites the whole result each time, which only makes sense when the result is small, such as one row per store. Not every query can use every mode. An aggregation without a watermark cannot run in append mode, and Spark refuses to start it with an analysis error rather than write nothing silently. A query with no aggregation at all cannot use complete mode, because there is no finite result to rewrite. The live sales job will use append, because its sink is a folder of Parquet files. Next, joining a stream to other data.

A stream can be joined to other data in two ways. The first is a stream-static join, on line fifteen: the orders stream joined to the stores table, which is read once as an ordinary DataFrame. Each micro-batch joins its new orders to the stores, exactly as the batch job did, and Spark keeps no state for it. That is how every order gets its city. The second is a stream-stream join, where both sides are unbounded. Payments arrive on their own stream, read on lines seventeen to nineteen, and the business wants to know which orders were paid. The difficulty is that an order and its payment may arrive in different batches, in either order, so Spark must keep both sides in state, waiting for a match. Without a limit, it would wait for ever. Lines twenty to twenty-three give it one. Both sides have a watermark, and the join condition says a payment must come between the order's time and thirty minutes after it. With that bound, Spark knows when an unmatched order can no longer find its payment, and can drop it from state. The terminal shows the matches. o one, placed at nine oh one, was paid at nine oh five, and matches in the first batch. o four, placed at nine fourteen and paid at nine twenty, matches once the second file brings the order in. o five was paid too, at ten past ten, but that is fifty-three minutes after it was placed, outside the thirty-minute bound, so this inner join never reports it. Whether that is right is a business question; an outer join would report o five as unpaid instead, once the watermark passes. The list sums up. Joining to a table is cheap and stateless. Joining two streams keeps both sides as state, and a time bound is what keeps that state finite. Next, the checkpoint that all of this state is kept in.

A streaming job will stop: for a deployment, a failure, a machine that is replaced. The checkpoint is what lets it start again where it was. This script runs the running totals in two separate processes. The first, with the argument first, starts from an empty checkpoint, on line fourteen, and processes the first two files. Then the process ends. The second, with the argument then, does not clear anything: it processes the last two files using the same checkpoint location. The terminal shows both runs. The first prints batches zero and one, with the totals we saw in section one. The second starts at batch two, not zero, and its totals carry straight on: store seven at a hundred and thirty, store nine at seventy-five, and then eighty. The new process did not re-read the first two files, and it did not lose their totals. Between the two runs, the terminal lists the checkpoint folder, and the table on the right says what each part holds. Metadata holds the query's id. Offsets holds the range of each batch, written before the batch runs. Commits records each batch that finished. Sources records the files the file source has already read. And state holds the running totals themselves, split into the partitions fixed at the first run. On restart, Spark compares offsets with commits: a batch that was planned but not committed is run again, with exactly the same range. The list covers the harder question, which changes a checkpoint survives. Adding a filter or a column that leaves the state alone usually works. Changing the aggregation, its keys, or the number of shuffle partitions does not: the state on disk no longer matches the query. Changing the source does not either. For those, the answer is a new checkpoint, and a plan for the data it will reprocess. Next, the crash that this replay exists for.

This section stages the failure that every streaming guarantee is about: a crash after the output is written, but before the batch is committed. Two foreach batch writers receive the same events. The first, on line twenty-seven, appends the batch's rows to a folder. The second, on line thirty-three, writes each batch into its own folder, named by batch id, in overwrite mode. Both call crash once, which raises an error the first time batch two has been written, before Spark can record the batch as committed. The loop at the bottom catches the crash and starts the query again, on line forty-five, with the same checkpoint. The terminal shows both queries terminating with an error, the restart, and then the count of rows each one left on disk. Spark did its part identically for both. The checkpoint said batch two was planned but never committed, so on restart the file source replayed it, with exactly the same files and exactly the same rows. What differed was the sink. The append writer had already written batch two's rows, and wrote them again: twelve rows on disk for ten events, with o six and o seven twice. The by batch writer replaced batch two's folder with the same contents: ten rows for ten events, as if the crash had never happened. That is the meaning of an idempotent sink. The list states the rule. A replayable source and a checkpoint give you every batch at least once; only the sink can turn at least once into exactly once, by making a second write of the same batch harmless. foreach batch gives you the batch id for exactly this purpose, and it is as safe as the code written in it. Spark's own file sink does this for you, by recording which batches it has committed. Next, everything in this course in a single run.

The last section puts the course together in one job, jobs slash live sales dot py, run the way it would run in production: started once for each delivery, and stopped when it has caught up. The run once function is the whole pipeline. Line seventeen reads the inbox and keeps completed orders that parsed. Lines eighteen and nineteen set a ten-minute watermark and drop duplicates within it, so a resent order counts once. Line twenty joins each order to its store's city, a stream-static join. Line twenty-one groups by ten-minute window of event time and city, and line twenty-six appends the result to a folder of Parquet files, with a checkpoint, using the available now trigger. tools slash feed dot py delivers the four files one by one and runs the job after each, four separate starts of the same query from the same checkpoint. Then it reads the output. The terminal shows the final table: four rows, each a window that the watermark has made final. Nine o'clock in Leeds: sixty-five pounds, from two orders. Nine o'clock in York: fifteen. Ten past in Hull: eighty, and ten past in York: sixty. The table on the right accounts for all ten events. o two's resend was dropped as a duplicate. o six and o eight are in windows the watermark has not yet passed, so they are still in state and will be written when later events move it on. And both late orders are missing, for two different reasons. o nine was too late for its window, as in section seven. o seven is the surprise: it is not here either, although the windows-only query in section seven kept it. In this job the deduplication runs first, and drop duplicates within watermark discards any event that is already older than the watermark when it arrives. o seven, at nine oh six, came in when the watermark was nine oh seven. Each operator applied the same ten-minute bound correctly; the order of operators decided the result. That is the real lesson of streaming: every late order is a decision someone made, and it should be made on purpose. Next, Course twelve: taking this pipeline to production.
